title: Montana Zyn Users Find 20 Pouches In New Cans - My 103.5
content: When I was younger, I was a Copenhagen Long Cut guy. And at one point, I was chewing AND smoking, sometimes simultaneously. Can you say addiction? Indeed. Eventually, when good old Cope started tearing up my lip, and I got tired of the stigma, cost, and smell of cigarettes, I quit both. I used the free nicotine gum from the Montana Quit program, and kicked the habit. That didn't last very long. I need nicotine! Of course, I don't. Nobody needs it. But here we are. Read More: A Very Riley Christmas - Win a $5,000 Amazon Shopping Spree I go through about a can a day. And if you do too, here's some fantastic news. The cans now have 20 pouches instead of 15. In the United States, about 794 million cans of Zyn were shipped in full-year 2025, up 37% from 2024, according to a CSP report. Based on Philip Morris International's 2026 trajectory, annual U.S. volumes are projected to exceed 700 million cans this year. The nicotine display at your favorite convenience store provides an overwhelming variety of pouch options. 3mg, 6mg, 9mg, even 12mg dosages are offered, along with more flavors than you can shake a stick at. Many of the Zyn imitators are cheaper, and almost all of them come with 20 pouches instead of Zyn's 15. I first noticed the fuller Zyn cans a week or so ago, thinking, "Huh, it seems like there are more in this can than usual." This week, an email from Zyn confirmed the news that I wasn't imagining things. The new 20-pouch cans are rolling out across Montana now. You might get some of the older, 15-count cans, but here's the nice surprise... the price is knocked down considerably. The old 15-count rolls of Zyn are now roughly $17 (depending on location/promo offers), instead of their usual $28+ price. And if your tab for a 5-can roll is closer to $30, that means you're getting one of the new 20-packs.

content: TSM stock slipped 4% below $350 after a 14% rebound on Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia. US export rules and the $336 support remain in focus. Nvidia’s board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO yesterday, less than two weeks after he was forced out. TSMC is a key manufacturing partner for Nvidia, so the news removed a major overhang from the AI chip chain. Volume in TSM was 100% above average yesterday, which means strong buying was seen after last week’s selloff. On the other hand, the stock opened near $385.49 and closed near the low of the day, which also means that there was some profit-taking at higher levels. That selling has carried into today’s session. Recently, TSMC said in a statement that it does not see a deeper correction in the AI market. The company said global AI demand continues to outstrip its supply of advanced chips. last week the stock fell sharply on AI worries, but the management is denying it and insisting of heavy demand in market. However, the new US export rule is still weighing on the stock. The rule took effect on 19th Nov and removes the exemption that let Chinese chip designers use overseas foundries without licenses. It also covers older nodes like 16nm and 14nm. Nikkei reported that TSMC put some shipments on hold, to both Chinese and non-Chinese designers. The reason is that it is still reviewing compliance. TSMC said it will comply but declined to confirm the reports of suspended orders. Meanwhile, Beijing threatened countermeasures. This means any confirmed order loss from China could add further pressure on the stock price. Yesterday, traders bought about 187,858 call options on TSM. This is +36% above the average daily call volume. At the same time, Taiwan loosened margin call rules after the Taiex fell -17% last week. In Taipei, TSMC added NT$5.2 T about $158 B in value today. The average Wall Street analysts consensus rating is Buy for the TSM stock with 20 Buy and 1 Hold ratings. The average price target by them is $586.69. The stock is trading below its 50-D moving average of $403.78 and its 200-D average of $409.62, and both averages are now turning lower. The initial support S1 is at $336.40 level, which lines up with the 2.0 Fibonacci extension at $335.85, with the next support S2 at $314.54 level near Friday’s low. On the upside, initial resistance R1 is at $364.87, the 1.618 Fibonacci extension, and the next resistance level R2 is at $390.78. Any close above $364.87 level could push TSM toward $390.78. On the other hand, any close below $336.40 level could drag the price towards $314.54 level. Momentum still favors sellers, with the RSI at 40.52 and the MACD below zero. The stock has also kept a pattern of lower highs since the October peak near $487.81. It was the largest one-day percentage gain since October 28, 2008, when the stock rose 21.07%, and ranks 11th since the ADR listed in October 1997. The rally reversed Friday's 9.48% drop to $318.71. Even after Monday, the stock closed 25% below its October 5 record close of $485.80 and was down 13.12% for the month. Tuesday's decline gives back 35% of Monday's gain, which makes TSMC one of the better-performing chip names on a day when Nvidia is down 8.27%, AMD is off 11.70%, Micron has lost 11.59% and Analog Devices has dropped 18.55%. The ADR is falling with the sector but holding a larger share of its Monday rally than the names that were bid up hardest. That relative strength fits the fundamentals: TSMC is the only company in the AI hardware chain that is guiding to accelerating revenue growth and a gross margin above 65% at the same time. The thesis for this forecast is that TSMC's operating trend is the strongest in semiconductors, but the stock trades as a high-beta AI proxy, and that proxy is under pressure from Nvidia's volatility, a new U.S. export rule on China and a market that has stopped rewarding hardware beats. October revenue rose 59.7% year on year to NT$586.89 billion. Fourth-quarter guidance calls for $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion, 58% growth at the midpoint. Against that, the stock trades at 18.9 times annualized third-quarter earnings. The near-term forecast is a $336 to $364 range into the holiday-thinned week, with a $395 upside target that becomes live only after a daily close above Monday's $363.60. The ADR's 2026 chart has three phases. The stock rallied through the summer to a record close of $485.80 on October 5. It then fell in stages through October and November, losing ground on the October 15 earnings report as margins narrowed and capex worries grew. It closed at $395.75 on November 4, down 2.24% on a day the S&P 500 rose 1.6%, after the midterm results raised concerns about data-center restrictions such as Texas's proposed moratorium. The decline sped up in the week of November 16, ending with the 9.48% drop to $318.71 on November 20, which left the stock 34.4% below its record. Monday's move was violent in both directions. The ADR opened with a gap higher and printed an intraday high of $386.90 early in the session, a 21.4% gain from Friday's close at the peak. It faded through the day to close at $363.60, near the $361.66 session low. Volume was 100% above average, and traders bought 187,858 call options. Monday's after-hours trade reached $368.69, up 1.40%. Tuesday morning gave that back before the open. The ADR slipped 2.78% to $353.50 in premarket trading by 8:44 a.m. ET, opened down 3.19% at $356.47, and then extended the decline below $350. At $347.93, the stock is 28.4% below its October 5 record, 9.2% above Friday's $318.71 close, and 15.4% higher for the year. Market value has dropped from $1.88 trillion at Monday's close to $1.78 trillion. The month-to-date decline is now 17% from the late-October level near $420. The near-term levels are close together. Support starts at $336, the first area where buyers stepped in during last week's selloff and the next technical shelf below the current price. Below that, $318.71 is Friday's close and the November low, and the line bulls must defend to keep Monday's reversal intact. A daily close below $318.71 would open a move toward $300, and toward the levels where the stock started the year. Resistance starts at $356.47, Tuesday's opening print, then $363.60 to $364.87, Monday's close and the first major ceiling. Above it, $368.69 marks Monday's after-hours peak. The $386.90 intraday high from Monday and the $390.78 technical level sit just above. The $395 upside target in this forecast aligns with the $395.75 November 4 close, the last stable level before the November breakdown. Getting there requires the ADR to clear Monday's close first, and that requires the AI hardware tape to stabilize. The Taiwan Stock Exchange posted its largest single-day point gain on record. The Taiex closed at 40,122.35, up 3,310.46 points or 8.99%, after trading between 39,148.91 and 40,180.48. That beat the previous record gain of 3,186.45 points set on July 31. At its peak the index was up 3,368.49 points, the largest intraday point gain on record. Turnover reached NT$419.41 billion, with 1,087 stocks rising and only 31 falling. Close to 600 listed companies touched their daily limit-up. TSMC drove the rally. It accounts for more than 40% of Taiwan's total stock market value, rose 9.85% shortly after the open and closed at the NT$2,230 limit price, contributing 1,600 points of the Taiex's gain on its own. The electronics index jumped 9.49%. MediaTek also rallied by close to 10%. Taiwan's move was the largest in Asia. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 3.9% to 58,644.63 after a three-day weekend, and South Korea's KOSPI jumped 6.2% to 6.3% to 5,006.03, with SK Hynix up 8.6% and Samsung Electronics up 8.2%. The context makes the gain look less like strength and more like a reversal. The Taiex lost 17.5% in the week of November 16 to November 20, its largest weekly decline since 1991. Over the weekend, regulators brought in market-stabilization measures, including a ban on short selling. The Taiwan Stock Exchange also cut the minimum maintenance ratio for margin accounts, effective November 24, which reduced forced selling from leveraged retail accounts. Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission kept three waves of market-rescue measures in place and said it was watching three indicators to decide when to lift them. That support matters for the stock. A short-selling ban and looser margin rules remove two sources of selling pressure in Taipei, but they also hide true price discovery. When the measures are lifted, some of today's buying may reverse. The New York ADR trades without those protections, which partly explains why it is falling on a day the Taipei shares closed limit-up. The parity math shows the listings are close to aligned. Each ADR represents five Taipei shares. At TSMC's NT$31.8 per dollar guidance exchange rate, the NT$2,230 Taipei close is worth $350.63 per ADR. At $347.93, the ADR trades at a 0.8% discount to Taipei. Usually the ADR trades at a premium. A discount means New York investors are more cautious than Taiwanese buyers, who are trading under protective market rules. TSMC's most recent quarter is the base for the bull case. According to its third-quarter 6-K filing, the company reported consolidated revenue of NT$1,494.24 billion, net income of NT$763.06 billion and diluted EPS of NT$29.43, or $4.60 per ADR unit, for the quarter ended September 30. Revenue rose 50.9% year on year, and net income and EPS each rose 68.7%. Against the second quarter, revenue grew 17.6% and net income 8.0%. It was the sixth straight record quarterly profit. In dollars, revenue was $46.72 billion, up 41.2% year on year and 16.2% sequentially. That beat the top of the company's own $44.6 billion to $45.8 billion guidance range. Gross margin was 66.4%, operating margin 58.7% and net margin 51.1%. Operating margin beat the top end of the 56.0% to 58.0% guidance. Gross profit was NT$992.38 billion, up 68.6% year on year. The technology mix shows why demand is concentrated at the leading edge. In the third quarter, 2nm wafers made up 8% of wafer revenue, 3nm accounted for 33%, 5nm 28% and 7nm 10%. Advanced technologies, defined as 7nm and below, made up 79% of wafer revenue, up from 77% in the second quarter. High-performance computing, which includes AI accelerators and data-center CPUs, rose to 68% of revenue. Management's message was unequivocal. Chief Executive C.C. Wei told analysts that the gap between demand and supply is still large and that the company saw no sign of slowdown. In July he described the gap as "very big," with 3nm lines running above 100% utilization and CoWoS advanced packaging remaining the industry's main bottleneck. He has also said AI demand will remain strong through 2030. TSMC's full-year 2026 dollar revenue growth is tracking 44%, up from an initial outlook of above 30% in January. The market sold the beat anyway. TSMC's shares fell after the October 15 report on margin and spending concerns, as Asian chip stocks sold off. That reaction foreshadowed the November pattern across semiconductors: strong results paired with any sign of margin pressure or higher capex now get sold. The third-quarter print showed record growth with a 1.3 point gross-margin decline. The market focused on the decline. The monthly numbers confirm the acceleration. TSMC's October revenue report shows consolidated revenue of NT$586.89 billion, up 14.7% from September and 59.7% from October 2025. Revenue for January through October totaled NT$4,485.62 billion, up 43.3% year on year. October was the largest single month in TSMC's history and the first above NT$550 billion. The monthly trend through 2026 shows steady gains. June revenue was NT$442.68 billion, up 67.9% year on year. July reached NT$467.58 billion, up 44.7%. August was NT$514.81 billion, up 53.3%. September was NT$511.86 billion, down 0.6% month on month but up 54.6% year on year. October's 14.7% sequential jump is the strongest month-on-month gain since the start of the year. The fourth-quarter guidance math looks achievable. TSMC guided fourth-quarter revenue to $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion at an exchange rate of NT$31.8 per dollar. That is a 14% sequential gain and 58% year-on-year growth at the midpoint. The $53.3 billion midpoint converts to NT$1,694.94 billion. October's NT$586.89 billion is 34.6% of that total in the first of three months. To hit the midpoint, November and December need to average NT$554.0 billion each, 5.6% below October's pace. To hit the top end of $54.3 billion, or NT$1,726.74 billion, the two months need to average NT$569.9 billion, still 2.9% below October. That puts TSMC on track for an upside surprise unless November and December revenue drop sharply. The main risk is the export rule that took effect November 19, which could reduce shipments to some Chinese customers in the second half of the month. China's share of TSMC's revenue has shrunk steadily as U.S. controls tightened, and the affected designers are a small share of the total. Even a full loss of those orders is unlikely to cost more than a few percentage points of fourth-quarter revenue. The November revenue report is due on December 10, one day after the Fed decision. A print above NT$570 billion would confirm the top end of guidance is in reach and would probably be the catalyst that sends the ADR back toward $395. A print below NT$530 billion would raise questions about whether the export rule or customer credit limits are biting, and would put $318.71 back in play. Margins are the main fundamental debate. Third-quarter gross margin of 66.4% was down 1.3 percentage points from 67.7% in the second quarter. Chief Financial Officer Wendell Huang attributed the decline primarily to dilution from the 2nm ramp. Fourth-quarter guidance calls for a gross margin of 65% to 67% and an operating margin of 56.5% to 58.5%. The 66% midpoint is a further 40 basis point decline, which the CFO attributed to continued dilution from the steep 2nm ramp and from overseas fabs. The 2nm cost structure is front-loaded. New nodes carry high depreciation and low initial yields, so margin dilution peaks in the first year of volume production and fades as yields improve and capacity utilization rises. TSMC has warned that the 2nm ramp will dilute full-year margins by 2 to 3 percentage points. 2nm capacity is expected to reach 100,000 wafers per month by year-end. As that capacity fills and yields improve in 2027, the dilution should narrow, as it did with the 3nm and 5nm ramps. Overseas fabs are a longer-lasting drag. TSMC has said its plants in Arizona and Japan will reduce gross margin by 3 to 4 percentage points over the next several years. Costs in the U.S. are higher because of labor, construction and supply chains, and those fabs start at lower volume. Unlike node dilution, overseas dilution does not fade as quickly. It narrows only as the fabs scale and TSMC passes some of the cost on through pricing. The margin picture explains why investors are cautious despite 58% revenue growth. HPE reported a 2.2 point sequential decline in adjusted gross margin on Monday and fell 13.14% on Tuesday. Analog Devices beat and fell 18.55% on a weaker margin outlook. The market is punishing any company whose AI revenue is growing faster than its profitability. TSMC is in the same category on paper, though its margin is in the mid-60s, far above HPE's. At 66%, TSMC's gross margin is higher than most software companies. Pricing power is the counterweight. TSMC raised wafer prices for advanced nodes in 2026, and demand still exceeds supply at 3nm and below. A company that sells out its leading-edge capacity can raise prices to offset dilution. If 2027 contract pricing comes in higher, as the demand-supply gap suggests, gross margin can hold in the mid-60s despite the 2nm and overseas drag. TSMC is spending at a record pace. The company raised its 2026 capital expenditure budget to $60 billion to $64 billion in July, up from $52 billion to $56 billion at the start of the year. It reiterated that range on the October 15 call. That is the first time annual capex has passed ¥10 trillion. In the second quarter alone, capex reached $15.7 billion. TSMC has said spending over the next three years will be "significantly higher" than the $101 billion it invested over the previous three. Arizona is the centerpiece. In July TSMC committed an additional $100 billion to Arizona for several more 2nm-and-below logic fabs and advanced-packaging facilities, taking its total U.S. investment to $265 billion and its planned U.S. footprint to 12 facilities. On the October call, Wei said the second Arizona fab is built and moving in tools, with volume production planned for the third quarter of 2027, slightly ahead of schedule. The U.S. investment is tied to trade policy. On January 16, 2026, Taiwan and the United States signed a trade agreement under which Taiwanese semiconductor and technology companies will invest $250 billion in the U.S. economy, and the U.S. lowered its tariff on Taiwanese exports from 20% to 15%. On July 24, the U.S. imposed an additional 10% tariff on Taiwan, citing alleged forced labor in the supply chain. Tuesday's premarket selling in chip stocks was also tied to a tariff report. Trade policy remains a live risk for TSMC's cost base and for its customers' pricing. The capex story has two readings. The bull reading is that TSMC is building capacity for demand that its customers have already committed to, and that each dollar of capex is backed by multi-year orders. The bear reading is that the AI build-out may peak before the new fabs are fully loaded, leaving TSMC with expensive overseas capacity and declining utilization. Capex planned in 2026 contributes little to 2026 output and only marginally to 2027, so the payoff depends on demand in 2028 and beyond. November's market moves show which reading dominates right now. Hardware stocks are being sold on doubts about the durability and returns of AI spending. TSMC's capex is the largest single bet on that durability in the industry. Until AI spending shows it can last into 2028, investors will discount TSMC's capex as a risk rather than value it as growth. A new U.S. rule hit TSMC last week. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security interim final rule, "Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors," took effect on November 19, 2026. Before that date, some Chinese AI chip designers could still order 7nm chips from TSMC through a verification mechanism. The rule removed that mechanism and moved the cutoff to 16nm. Under the rule, 16nm- and 14nm-class logic chips are presumed advanced, and a manufacturer overriding that presumption must now meet conditions on the designer's location and ultimate parent. TSMC responded quickly. It told affected Chinese customers to stop placing orders at 16nm and more advanced nodes unless they hold U.S. export licenses, and told staff to suspend some existing orders until licenses are obtained. Approved U.S. designers, a list that includes no mainland Chinese firms, keep full access. Samsung took similar action. Under the rule, new reporting applies to exports made on or after November 19, 2026. The timing fed last week's selloff. The rule took effect on Thursday, the halted orders were reported Friday morning, and the ADR fell 9.48% that day. The Affiliates Rule, which extends export restrictions to any foreign entity owned 50% or more by an Entity List company, had been suspended for one year starting November 10, 2025. That suspension has now expired, adding to the compliance burden for foundries serving Chinese customers. The revenue impact is limited but not zero. China's share of TSMC's revenue has fallen as U.S. controls tightened, and most of its leading-edge output goes to U.S. designers such as Nvidia, Apple, AMD and Broadcom. The affected Chinese AI designers are a small share of the total. The bigger risk is precedent. Every new rule shrinks TSMC's addressable market in China, and Chinese customers that lose access to TSMC accelerate domestic alternatives, which could compete with TSMC at mature nodes over time. For the forecast, the export rule is a known headwind, not a new shock. It is already reflected in Friday's 9.48% drop. Any confirmed order losses from China would weigh on November and December revenue. If TSMC's November revenue on December 10 shows no meaningful drop, the rule will fade as a concern and remove one of the overhangs holding the stock below $364. TSMC's stock is tied to Nvidia, its largest customer for AI accelerators. Nvidia's leadership crisis drove much of November's chip selloff. Huang resigned on November 12, and the board said on November 17 it did not intend to reinstate him. TSMC's Taipei shares fell through the period, and the Taiex had its worst week since 1991. Monday's reinstatement reversed the move. Nvidia rose 31.48% to $165.05, adding $952 billion in market value, and TSMC rose 14.08%. Tuesday shows the link working in reverse. Nvidia is down 8.27%, trading near $151. AMD has dropped 11.70%, Micron 11.59%, Broadcom 4.50% and Intel 5.80%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index is down 6.17% at 8,996.18, and SMH has lost 8.29%. TSMC's 4.31% decline is roughly half of Nvidia's and a third of AMD's. The stock is falling with the group but by less, as befits the company with the clearest earnings visibility in the chain. Nvidia's own results support TSMC's demand outlook. Last week, Nvidia reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, with data-center revenue of $107.6 billion, and guided fourth-quarter revenue to $130 billion. Nvidia does not manufacture its own chips. Almost all of that revenue runs through TSMC's 3nm and 4nm lines and its CoWoS packaging. A guide to $130 billion is a guide to higher TSMC wafer and packaging orders into early 2027. The AI hardware tape is the problem. Investors are no longer paying for hardware beats. HPE grew fourth-quarter revenue 50% and fell 13.14%. Analog Devices reported a record year and fell 18.55%. Semtech beat and raised and fell 14.17%. Anthropic's IPO, which priced at $83 on November 18, fell below its offer price on Tuesday. The market is questioning the returns on AI spending, and every hardware supplier is being sold, regardless of execution. TSMC also reportedly set credit limits for AI customers in a November 18 report. That suggests the company is managing counterparty risk among smaller AI chip designers whose funding depends on capital markets. Credit discipline protects TSMC's balance sheet but caps growth from customers whose demand depends on venture funding. If the AI funding cycle tightens, TSMC will see it first in those customers' orders. TSMC's competitive position has never been stronger at the leading edge. It holds the large majority of the foundry market for 3nm and below. Its 2nm process entered volume production in 2026, reaching 8% of wafer revenue in the third quarter, and capacity is planned to reach 100,000 wafers per month by year-end. No competitor has a 2nm process in comparable high-volume production. Samsung is the closest foundry competitor. Its shares rose 6.7% to 8.2% in Seoul on Tuesday, along with the rest of the Korean chip complex. Samsung's foundry business has struggled with yields at advanced nodes and has lost share to TSMC at 3nm. The new U.S. export rule hits Samsung the same way, since Samsung also suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers while it applies for export licenses. Samsung's strength is in memory, where it competes with SK Hynix for high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. SK Hynix rose 8.6% in Seoul on Tuesday, but its U.S.-listed shares are down 9.01% in New York. That is the same split TSMC is showing. Memory stocks are seeing the deepest give-back in the U.S. session. Micron has given back more than 70% of its 19.04% Monday gain. Memory pricing is tied to the AI build-out, but memory is a more cyclical business than foundry, and investors are trimming the most cyclical exposure first. Intel Foundry is the long-term U.S. alternative. Intel shares are down 5.80% on Tuesday. Intel's foundry ambitions depend on its 18A process and on winning external customers, and it remains years behind TSMC in leading-edge foundry share. TSMC's $265 billion Arizona build-out has reduced the strategic case for Intel as a domestic alternative, since TSMC's U.S. fabs give American customers onshore supply at TSMC's process quality. The competitive gap is a key reason TSMC holds up better than peers on down days. TSMC's pricing power comes from having no direct rival at 2nm and 3nm. Samsung and Intel compete at the margins, and memory companies serve a different part of the AI stack. When investors cut AI hardware exposure, TSMC is the last position they sell, because it is the one with the least competitive risk. That is reflected in Tuesday's 4.31% decline against an 8% to 12% drop for Nvidia, AMD and Micron. TSMC's valuation is moderate for its growth rate. Third-quarter EPS was $4.60 per ADR. Annualized, that is $18.40 per ADR. At $347.93, the ADR trades at 18.9 times run-rate earnings. The fourth-quarter guide implies further EPS growth: a 14% sequential revenue increase at a 57.5% operating margin would lift fourth-quarter ADR EPS above $5.00. On a forward run rate of $20.00, the ADR trades at 17.4 times earnings. Those multiples are low against the growth rate. Revenue is growing 58% year on year at the fourth-quarter guidance midpoint, and net income grew 68.7% in the third quarter. A price-to-earnings-to-growth ratio below 0.5 is rare for a company with TSMC's market share and margins. Nvidia trades at a higher multiple. Analog Devices traded near 49 to 50 times trailing earnings before its 18.55% drop. TSMC is the cheapest large-cap AI hardware stock on earnings. The discount reflects risks that are hard to model. Geopolitical risk around Taiwan is the largest. TSMC's Taiwan fabs produce most of the world's leading-edge chips, and any disruption in the Taiwan Strait would be catastrophic for the company and the global supply chain. Investors apply a permanent discount for that risk, and the discount widens during periods of U.S.-China tension, such as the current export rule. Market value gives another reference point. At $347.93, TSMC is worth $1.78 trillion, against $1.88 trillion at Monday's close and $2.5 trillion at the October 5 record. The NT$5.2 trillion added in Taipei on Tuesday shows how quickly value moves in this stock. A return to the $395 upside target would add $250 billion to the market value. Historical patterns support buying deep drawdowns. TSMC's largest one-day gains, including Monday's 14.08% and the 21.07% in October 2008, have come near cycle lows when sentiment toward semiconductors was at its worst. The stock is up 15.4% year to date even after a 28.4% drawdown from its record. Investors who held from January have no loss. Those who bought between August and October are underwater and are the likely sellers on rallies toward $395 to $420. The technical setup is a reversal pattern that has not yet been confirmed. Friday's $318.71 close marked the November low after a 34.4% decline from the record. Monday's 14.08% gap higher on 100% above-average volume is the kind of move that often marks a turning point. But the $386.90 intraday high faded into a close near the session low, and Tuesday's follow-through is lower. A reversal is confirmed when the stock closes above the reversal day's high or holds above its midpoint. Monday's midpoint between $361.66 and $386.90 is $374.28, and the stock is well below it. Options positioning shows that traders are betting on a rebound. Monday's 187,858 call contracts traded far exceeded normal call volume, with strikes concentrated above $364. Implied volatility is elevated after a 14% daily move and will likely stay high through the November revenue report on December 10. High implied volatility makes call options expensive, so traders betting on a rebound are paying up for the right. The calendar is crowded. U.S. markets close on Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early on Friday, while Taipei trades normally, so TSMC's Taipei shares will trade two sessions without a New York reference. Wednesday brings the October PCE report and third-quarter GDP revision, which will move rate expectations and growth stocks. Dell reports after Tuesday's close, with consensus at $6.55 EPS on $49.24 billion of revenue. Its server margin will be read across to the whole AI hardware supply chain. The Fed decides on December 9, with a 95.1% probability of a 25 basis point hike priced in. TSMC's November revenue report on December 10 is the most important company-specific catalyst. It will show whether the export rule has hit shipments and whether the fourth-quarter top-end guidance is in reach. TSMC's fourth-quarter results in mid-January will include 2027 guidance for revenue growth, gross margin and capex. Investors will focus on whether 2027 capex rises above $64 billion and whether margins stabilize. The level map is straightforward. Support at $336 is the first test. A break below it opens $318.71, the November low. Resistance at $356.47 is Tuesday's opening print. Above it, $363.60 to $364.87 is Monday's close and the first major ceiling. The $374.28 midpoint of Monday's range and the $386.90 high come next. The $395 target sits at the $395.75 November 4 close. TSMC heads into the Thanksgiving week as the strongest fundamental story in semiconductors, trading on the sector's weakest tape. The near-term forecast is a $336 to $364 range through the December 10 November revenue report, with a $395 upside target that becomes live only after a daily close above Monday's $363.60. Support starts at $336, the first shelf below the current price. Below it, $318.71 is Friday's close and the November low, the line that has to hold to keep Monday's reversal valid. A daily close below $318.71 would open a move toward $300, near where the stock started 2026, and would cancel out Monday's 14.08% best-since-2008 rally. Resistance starts at $356.47, Tuesday's open. The $363.60 to $364.87 band is Monday's close and the key pivot. Above it, $368.69 marks Monday's after-hours high, $374.28 the midpoint of Monday's range, and $386.90 the intraday high. The $395 upside target aligns with the $395.75 November 4 close, the last level before the November breakdown. Reaching it requires the semiconductor index to stabilize, November revenue above NT$570 billion, and no further escalation of the export rule. The fundamental case is the strongest in the sector. Third-quarter revenue was $46.72 billion, above guidance. October revenue was a record NT$586.89 billion, up 59.7% year on year. Fourth-quarter guidance of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion implies 58% growth at the midpoint, and October alone delivered 34.6% of that target. Gross margin is 66.4%, net margin 51.1%. Advanced technologies are 79% of wafer revenue and high-performance computing 68% of revenue. Capex of $60 billion to $64 billion and a $265 billion Arizona plan show management's confidence in demand through 2030. The stock trades at 18.9 times annualized third-quarter earnings. The risks are real but mostly known. A 16nm export cutoff on Chinese AI designers took effect November 19. Gross margin faces 2nm ramp dilution and 3 to 4 points of overseas drag. The AI hardware tape is punishing beats across the sector. Taiwan's market is running under a short-selling ban and looser margin rules, and Taiwan carries geopolitical risk. The verdict on November 24 is a strong business in a weak tape. TSMC at $347.93 is a buy-the-$336 to $318 zone, sell-the-$364 ceiling market until the November revenue report confirms the fourth-quarter trajectory. A clean November print and a stable AI hardware tape turn $364 into the launch point for $395. A break below $318.71 would mean the sector selloff is overriding TSMC's fundamentals, and would put $300 in play.

title: TSM's AI-Driven Growth Accelerates: Is There More Upside Ahead? - The Globe and Mail
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company LimitedTSM continues to benefit from growing investment in AI infrastructure as it drives demand for advanced semiconductor technologies. The company's third-quarter 2026 performance reflected this momentum, with revenues increasing 41.2% year over year to $46.72 billion. High-performance computing (HPC) contributed 68% of total revenues, increasing 22% sequentially. The growing adoption of advanced manufacturing technologies also supported performance, with 2-nanometer technology accounting for 8% of wafer revenues, compared with 3% in the preceding quarter. Management expects full-year 2026 revenues to grow approximately 44% in U.S. dollar terms, reflecting sustained demand across its portfolio.TSM's growth opportunity extends beyond conventional AI accelerators. The company highlighted increasing demand associated with agentic AI, server processors and networking chips, which could broaden semiconductor requirements across data-center infrastructure. The company had previously projected a mid-to-high-50% compound annual growth rate for AI accelerator revenue between 2024 and 2029. However, TSM has now indicated that demand could potentially exceed that outlook.TSM is steadily expanding its manufacturing capabilities to capture these opportunities. Its N2-family annual capacity is expected to more than double in 2027. The company is also preparing for A14 technology, with volume production planned for 2028. These developments strengthen its position in the advanced semiconductor manufacturing market. United Microelectronics CorporationUMC, another semiconductor foundry operator, is witnessing improving demand across its technology portfolio. UMC’s third-quarter 2026 revenues increased 25.6% year over year to NT$74.24 billion, while capacity utilization reached 92%. Its 22-nanometer technology accounted for a record 18.3% of wafer sales, supported by customer demand for display drivers, automotive radar and Wi-Fi integrated circuits. UMC is also pursuing opportunities in advanced packaging and silicon photonics, which could support additional growth as AI infrastructure requirements increase.Intel CorporationINTC is also witnessing stronger demand across its data-center and AI operations. Intel’s third-quarter 2026 revenues increased 21% year over year to $16.5 billion, while Data Center and AI revenues surged 78% to $7.3 billion. Intel's Foundry segment generated $6.7 billion in revenues, increasing 58% year over year, including intersegment transactions. Intel is seeing robust demand for its Xeon processors and improving manufacturing execution. However, supply constraints remain a near-term challenge. TSM has gained 27.8% over the past year against the sector’s decline of 5.8%. From a valuation standpoint, TSM trades at a forward price-to-sales ratio of 8.41, above the industry’s 7.38. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for TSM’s earnings for 2026 has been raised 4.9% over the past 60 days. TSM currently carries a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy). title: TSM Stock: TSMC Jumps 10% to Its NT$2,230 Limit as the Taiex Soars 9% on Huang’s Return - FinanceFeeds
content: Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC) rose NT$200, or 9.85%, to NT$2,230 in Taipei on Tuesday, its daily limit, and held there through the session. Taiwan caps daily moves at 10%, and the limit price rounds down to the exchange’s NT$5 price step, so the cap worked out to 9.85% for TSM stock. The Taiex closed up 3,310.46 points, or 8.99%, at 40,122.35, Focus Taiwan reported. The move followed a 31.48% jump in Nvidia stock to $165.05 on Monday after its board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. That rally added about $950 billion to Nvidia’s market value, by FinanceFeeds’ calculation. TSM stock had already climbed 13.93% to $363.60 in New York on Monday, according to TradingView. It traded at $370.41, up 1.87%, in overnight trading early Tuesday ET. TSMC, which accounts for over 40% of the Taiwan market’s total value, contributed about 1,600 points to the index’s rise in the morning session, Focus Taiwan reported. The limit-up move added NT$5.2 trillion, or $158 billion, to TSMC’s market value in one day, Fortune reported. More than 500 stocks on the main board and the over-the-counter market rose 10% in the morning, Focus Taiwan said. MediaTek hit its NT$4,050 limit and ASE Technology its NT$530 limit during that session, the agency reported. In the morning, the Taiex rose as much as 3,368.49 points, the largest intraday point gain in its history, according to CNA. Its 9.15% intraday rise was the second-largest percentage gain on record, behind the 9.39% of 10 April 2025, the agency said. The Taiex lost 7,641.83 points, or 17.5%, last week, its largest weekly point loss ever, Focus Taiwan reported. Even after Tuesday, the index sits about 20% below its intraday high of 49,968.92 on 6 October, by FinanceFeeds’ calculation. Taiwan’s Financial Supervisory Commission banned short selling of stocks that fell in the prior session on 21 November, and a lower margin maintenance ratio took effect on Tuesday. TSMC’s 2025 financial report shows its largest client, “Customer A,” paid NT$726.9 billion, or 19% of revenue, up from 12% a year earlier, Taiwan News reported. TSMC does not name the client, but Huang has said Nvidia became TSMC’s top customer, the report noted. That concentration ties TSM stock closely to Nvidia’s leadership and spending plans. TSMC’s October 2026 revenue reached NT$586.89 billion, up 59.7% from a year earlier, the company said in a filing with the SEC. January to October revenue rose 43.3% to NT$4,485.62 billion. Investors had feared the AI industry would lose momentum without Huang after he resigned on 12 November, The Motley Fool wrote. The reversal also lifted Jensen Huang’s net worth by about $34 billion on Forbes’ tracker on Monday. TSMC rose 9.85% to its NT$2,230 limit in Taipei, adding about $158 billion in value, after TSM stock gained 13.93% in New York on Monday. Monday’s NYSE close of $363.60 for TSM stock stood 17.8% above the value of the five Taipei shares behind each ADR at Monday’s NT$2,030 close, by FinanceFeeds’ calculation using Focus Taiwan’s exchange rates. After Tuesday’s limit-up close, that premium narrowed to about 7.4%. That is close to the 7.4% decade average for the ADR premium that Bloomberg data showed in August 2025. Taipei caught up with New York, so Tuesday’s local rally mostly reflected gains TSM stock had already booked on Monday. In overnight trading at $370.41, TSM stock sat about 9.4% above Tuesday’s Taipei close, by the same calculation. TSMC told affected Chinese customers to halt orders using processes of 16 nanometers and below unless they obtain US export licenses, people familiar with the matter said. New Commerce Department rules took effect on 19 November, and they apply to TSMC whether investors hold its Taipei shares or TSM stock. On Monday the department added seven companies to its Entity List, including Megaspeed, according to Fortune. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer has vowed an investigation into Huang’s return, and Nvidia’s independent board committee is still reviewing his conduct. TSMC published its October sales on 10 November, so the November figures for TSMC stock holders should arrive around 10 December. TradingView lists 21 January for its fourth-quarter report, with a consensus estimate of $52.65 billion in revenue. TSMC guided for $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion in October, Focus Taiwan reported.
